A lanai is a covered, open-air porch or veranda that is attached to a house or building. Think of it as a transitional space — it's not fully indoors (it doesn't have walls all around it), and it's not fully outdoors either (it has a roof over it). It sits right at the boundary between the two.

A lanai typically has:

  • A roof — this is what separates it from a plain open patio. The roof provides shade and shelter from rain.
  • Open or partially open sides — instead of solid walls, a lanai is open to the outside air, or may have railings, columns, screens, or partial walls. This is what makes it feel "outdoor."
  • A floor — usually made of tile, concrete, stone, or wood.
  • Furniture — chairs, sofas, tables, and sometimes even outdoor kitchens or ceiling fans, because it is treated as a genuine living area.

It is almost always attached directly to the house, and you typically walk out onto it through a door from inside.

A lanai is an outdoor living space. People use it to:

  • Sit and relax while enjoying the breeze and views
  • Have meals or entertain guests
  • Read, work, or simply spend time outside without being fully exposed to the sun or rain
  • Sometimes swim nearby, as lanais are very commonly built around pools

Because it is sheltered but open to the air, it lets you enjoy the feeling of being outside while staying comfortable. In warm, sunny, or humid climates, this makes a lanai enormously practical and pleasant.

The word is most closely associated with Hawaii, where this style of outdoor living space has been a central feature of homes for a very long time. The climate there — warm, breezy, with regular tropical showers — makes a covered-but-open porch ideal.

The term is also widely used in Florida, where the weather is similarly warm. In Florida, a lanai is often a screened enclosure — a porch enclosed not with walls but with fine mesh screens that keep out insects while still letting in air and light. Floridian lanais are frequently built around a swimming pool.

Beyond Hawaii and Florida, the word is used across the United States (and increasingly elsewhere) to refer to any covered outdoor living space of this style, especially in warmer regions.
How a lanai differs from similar spaces

Since the word belongs to a family of related terms, it helps to understand the distinctions clearly.

Lanai vs. patio
A patio is an outdoor area that is usually at ground level and open to the sky — no roof. A lanai always has a roof. So the key difference is that a lanai is covered; a patio is not.

Lanai vs. porch
A porch is a general term for a covered structure attached to the front, back, or side of a house. A lanai is essentially a type of porch, but the word carries the specific connotation of a Hawaiian or tropical-style space — more spacious, more deliberately furnished as a living area, and oriented toward outdoor leisure. In everyday American English, many people use "porch" and "lanai" loosely to mean similar things, but "lanai" implies a more generous, livable, tropical-flavored space.

Lanai vs. veranda
A veranda is also a roofed, open-sided porch, often wrapping around multiple sides of a house. A lanai and a veranda are very similar in concept. The difference is mainly cultural and regional: "veranda" is more common in British English and in South Asian or Australian contexts, while "lanai" is specifically Hawaiian in origin and most common in American English, particularly in warm-climate states.

Lanai vs. balcony
A balcony projects outward from an upper floor of a building and has no connection to the ground. A lanai, by contrast, is usually at or near ground level and is more of a porch than an elevated platform. The two are quite different in structure and feel.

Lanai vs. sunroom
A sunroom (also called an enclosed porch or Florida room) has glass walls and a roof, making it a fully enclosed glass-walled room. A lanai is open or screened — it allows actual air flow. A sunroom is essentially indoors; a lanai is essentially outdoors, just sheltered.

A lanai is a covered outdoor living space attached to a home — roofed but open or screened on the sides — designed for relaxing, dining, and spending time in the open air without being fully exposed to sun and rain. It is most at home in warm, tropical climates like Hawaii and Florida, and it represents a philosophy of living that blurs the line between indoors and outdoors.
